items.name: Headlamps
items.need: When the power is out, stairwells and corridors in a tall building can be fully dark once the emergency lights run down, and a headlamp gives each person light while keeping both hands free for the handrail, bags or a child.
items.how_to_choose: Know what powers the lamp, and keep spare cells or a way to recharge it. Some headlamps run on AAA cells, some on a rechargeable battery charged by USB, and some on either (often called dual-fuel or hybrid). A lamp that takes AAA cells keeps going as long as you have spares; a rechargeable lamp is usually brighter and runs longer on a charge, and in a long outage it needs a power bank. Look at the runtime on the medium setting, not the top lumen number: about 100 to 200 lumens is plenty for stairs and rooms, and the highest mode drains batteries in two to four hours. A lock function stops the lamp switching on inside a bag. Water resistance of IPX4 is enough indoors; a higher rating only matters if you will be out in heavy rain.

qty.note: One for each adult and teenager aged 14 or over; add one for each younger child old enough to wear one. A carried baby or toddler needs none.

items.already_own: Any working LED headlamp from camping, running or DIY is good enough. Know what it runs on: keep spare cells for one that takes AAA or AA cells, and a cable and a power bank for one that recharges. Test it now: put in fresh batteries or charge it, leave it on medium for an hour and check that it stays bright and the strap still holds.

safety_notes.text: Use flashlights and headlamps, not candles, when the power is out. US fire data counts about 20 home candle fires reported every day on average.
Official outage guidance is to have a flashlight for every member of the household and to plan for batteries or other backup power.

items.name: Handheld flashlights
items.need: A handheld flashlight throws light further than a headlamp for checking a dark corridor, a fuse panel or a stairwell landing, and it is the light you can hand to a neighbor or leave by the door.
items.how_to_choose: Know what cells a flashlight takes, and stock spares or a way to recharge it. A light that runs on AA cells shares spares with other gear. A light built around a rechargeable lithium-ion cell is usually brighter and runs longer on a charge, and it tops up from a power bank by USB-C; its spare is a second cell of the same kind. Some lights take both. A low mode of 30 to 100 lumens that lasts many hours matters more than a very high top number. Some lights stand on their tail to light a room off the ceiling and some do not; each pick's notes say which.

qty.note: Two per household: one by the front door and one by the bed.

items.already_own: Any LED flashlight that works will do. Know what cells it takes (AAA, AA, C, D, CR123A or a rechargeable lithium-ion cell) and keep spares, or the charging cable, with it. Check that the batteries have not leaked, fit fresh ones, and make sure it has a low mode. An old bulb flashlight that takes D cells still works; it is dimmer and heavier than an LED light, and it needs its own D cells.

safety_notes.text: Use flashlights, not candles, if the power goes out.
A basic emergency kit should include a flashlight and extra batteries.

item_flags: Counterfeit brand-name flashlights are sold on marketplaces. Buy from the maker or a seller the maker lists.

items.name: Room lanterns
items.need: A lantern lights a whole room evenly for cooking, eating and reading through long evenings without power, which a flashlight beam does badly.
items.how_to_choose: Look at how long it runs on a low or medium setting, because that is how it will be used for hours each night. Then look at what it runs on. A lantern on D cells runs longest and needs nothing kept charged, but it is heavy and needs its own stock of D cells. A rechargeable lantern can be topped up from a power bank or power station and needs a top-up every few months in storage. A small lantern on AAA or AA cells shares cells with headlamps and flashlights and lights a small room. A built-in solar panel only helps if you have a window that gets direct sun, and even then a full charge takes two or more sunny days.

qty.note: Two per household: one for the main room and one for the bathroom or a bedroom.

items.already_own: Any battery or rechargeable LED camping lantern is fine if it still holds a charge or takes cells you stock. Charge it fully, run it on low for an evening and note how long it lasts. Fuel-burning lanterns are not covered here; this list is for battery lights only.

safety_notes.text: Use battery lights, not candles, during an outage. About 20 home candle fires are reported each day on average in the US.

A rechargeable lantern recalled in January 2026 had lithium-ion batteries that could overheat and burn the user. Check any rechargeable lantern you own against the CPSC recall list, and stop using it at once if it has been recalled.

Follow the recall notice, and ask your local household hazardous-waste center whether it takes recalled lithium batteries before you carry one there. Treat a damaged one (swollen, cracked, leaking or hot) the same way.

items.name: Disposable batteries
items.need: Headlamps, flashlights, lanterns and radios are only useful while they have power, and sealed disposable cells are the one supply that sits ready for years with no charging.
items.how_to_choose: Count what cells each device takes before you buy, and stock spares for each kind: AAA, AA, C, D, 9 V, CR123A and coin cells are all different sizes, and none stands in for another. A lantern that takes D cells needs its own D cells: the Standard lantern here takes six. Buy name-brand cells with a printed use-by date and store them in their packaging at room temperature. Alkaline cells are cheap and keep for years: Energizer gives up to 15 years in storage for its MAX AA and AAA cells, up to 10 for C and D, and up to 5 for 9 V. They can leak inside devices, so store them outside the device. Lithium AA and AAA cells (lithium iron disulfide) cost several times more, but they keep for about 25 years, weigh less, work in the cold and are sold as leak proof; check each device's manual first, because some makers advise against them. The picks are priced as sets of AA and AAA cells because those are the sizes most small lights and radios take; the same alkaline brands sell C, D and 9 V cells.

qty.note: Count the cells in every light, lantern and radio you own, each size on its own line, and keep twice that number spare. Example: two headlamps that each take three AAA cells hold six cells between them, so keep twelve spare AAA cells. A lantern that takes six D cells needs twelve spare D cells. A light with a built-in rechargeable battery needs a way to charge it, not spare cells.

items.already_own: Check the date printed on any batteries you have. Unopened name-brand alkaline cells inside their date are fine. Throw out any with white crust or dampness, and do not mix old and new cells in one device.

safety_notes.text: Store batteries in a cool, dry place at normal room temperature. Do not mix old and new cells or different types in one device, and take batteries out of devices that will sit unused, because exhausted cells can leak or rupture.
Do not carry or store loose batteries with metal objects such as coins or keys; a short circuit can cause high heat or leakage. Keep loose cells in their packaging or a plastic case.
A device left switched on with dead alkaline cells can start to corrode in as little as two weeks. Remove spent cells promptly.

None of the picks on this page use button or coin cells. If other devices in your home do, keep those batteries away from small children: federal law (Reese's Law) now requires child-resistant battery compartments and warning labels on products that use them.

safety_notes.text: Lithium-ion batteries, such as those in power banks, rechargeable lanterns and headlamp packs, do not go in the trash: take an ordinary used one to a battery recycling location.

A recalled lithium battery is different. It does not go in the trash, in curbside recycling or in a store's battery box: follow the recall notice, and ask your local household hazardous-waste center whether it takes recalled lithium batteries before you carry one there. Treat a damaged one (swollen, cracked, leaking or hot) the same way.

items.name: Rechargeable AA/AAA batteries and charger
items.need: In an outage that lasts longer than the disposable stash, rechargeable cells can be refilled again and again from a power bank, a power station or a neighbor's working outlet.
items.how_to_choose: Choose low-self-discharge nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) cells, which hold most of their charge for years on the shelf. Pick a charger that charges each cell separately and stops when it is full. A charger with a USB input runs straight from a power bank or a power station's USB port; a wall-plug charger needs the power station's AC outlet, which wastes more of its stored energy. Count what your devices take first. The chargers and cells here cover AA and AAA sizes only, so a light that runs on C or D cells, such as a D-cell lantern, still needs disposable cells. Every kit here comes with AA cells; add a pack of rechargeable AAA cells if your lights use them.

qty.note: Optional extra: no baseline quantity. If you add it, buy one charger and count the cells the same way as for disposable ones: the cells in every light and radio you own, AA and AAA separately. Example: two headlamps that each take three AAA cells need six rechargeable AAA cells to fill them once.

items.already_own: Any name-brand NiMH AA or AAA cells and a charger with a separate light for each cell are good enough. Old cells that go dead within days of charging, or a timer-only charger with no per-cell shutoff, are worth replacing.

safety_notes.text: Only recharge cells that are marked rechargeable. Trying to recharge ordinary alkaline or lithium disposable cells can make them leak or rupture.
Do not mix battery types, such as alkaline and NiMH, or old and new cells, in one device. The weaker cells can be driven into reverse, which causes corrosion and gas.

items.name: Emergency radio with NOAA weather band
items.need: When cell networks are jammed or down, broadcast radio and NOAA Weather Radio are how officials tell you what is happening, where to go and when power or water will return.
items.how_to_choose: Get a radio that receives AM, FM and the seven NOAA weather channels, and know what powers it: cells you can replace, a built-in battery you recharge by USB, or both. An alert function sounds an alarm when the National Weather Service sends a warning on your local channel. What testers measured from hand cranks and solar panels: GearJunkie got about nine minutes of radio from one minute of cranking, and about 45 minutes from an hour of direct sun, on the Midland ER310PRO, and about five minutes per minute of cranking on the Sangean MMR-88. Bob Vila got about nine minutes per minute of cranking on the Midland ER310. That is enough to hear a forecast with no other power, and a slow way to fill a battery. County codes: none of the picks here has SAME county coding. They sound for every warning on the channel they are tuned to, which covers the whole broadcast area, and they never ask for a county code. A radio with SAME (Specific Area Message Encoding) lets you enter your county's code so that it sounds only for your area; those are mostly desktop radios that run from the wall with battery backup. Midland's WR120 is one, and GearJunkie's review of it says it does not receive AM or FM. If you want county-only alerts, add one of those, and look for the Public Alert or NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards logo that the National Weather Service recommends.
items.already_own: Any battery radio that gets AM and FM is useful for local news. Check whether it also has a weather band (marked WX or 162 MHz). If it does and it works on fresh batteries, it is good enough. A car radio also works, if your car is parked where you can reach it.

safety_notes.text: NOAA Weather Radio is a nationwide network of more than 1,000 transmitters that broadcasts official warnings, watches and forecasts 24 hours a day on seven VHF frequencies from 162.400 to 162.550 MHz. It covers non-weather emergencies too, and needs a receiver built to pick it up.
Find the transmitter and frequency for your area with the National Weather Service station search, then tune the radio to it and test it before you need it.

Weather Radio broadcasts cannot be heard on a plain AM/FM radio. The National Weather Service recommends receivers that carry the Public Alert or NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards logo, and notes that battery backup is important because outages often come with storms. It also explains SAME (Specific Area Message Encoding): a receiver that has it lets you choose the area you want alerts for, so it does not sound for warnings in other counties.
The federal emergency kit list includes a battery-powered or hand crank radio and a NOAA Weather Radio with tone alert.

items.name: Plug-in power-failure lights
items.need: A plug-in light that switches on by itself when the power fails means the first seconds of an outage are not spent in the dark hunting for a flashlight, and it lifts out of the outlet to use as one.
items.how_to_choose: Because these stay plugged into the wall all year, only buy one that carries a UL or ETL listing mark on the product itself, and check the mark when it arrives. Put them where the first steps matter: the hallway, by the bed and near the front door. Some models only come on in an outage if their switch is left in the right position, so read the instructions and test by switching off the breaker or unplugging the light. Units with a sealed rechargeable battery wear out after some years; test them twice a year.

qty.note: Two per household: one in the hallway and one in the main bedroom.

items.already_own: If you already have plug-in power-failure lights, look for the UL or ETL mark on the back, then unplug each one: it should light at once and stay bright for at least an hour. Replace any that fail, get hot or have no listing mark.

safety_notes.text: Use flashlights, not candles, if the power goes out.

Plug-in night lights have been recalled for overheating. One example: about 260,000 Energizer rotating LED night lights sold at Target were recalled in 2012 because they could overheat and smoke. Check any plug-in light you own against the CPSC recall list.
